interactions: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime: no clinically relevant interaction with spironolactone, furosemide, propranolol, lactulose, allopurinol or pantoprazole
Spironolactone and furosemide during SBP: added risk of hyponatremia and of kidney injury; hold diuretics while infection is treated and monitor sodium and creatinine
Propranolol during SBP: reduce or stop if systolic BP falls below 90 mmHg, sodium falls below 130 mEq/L or kidney injury develops; beta-blockade also blunts the heart-rate response to infection
Pantoprazole: long-term proton pump inhibitor use is associated with SBP and hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis; review the indication
Allopurinol: renally cleared; reduce the dose if creatinine rises
output.proposed: Ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) and IV albumin for SBP in cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy; current spironolactone, furosemide, propranolol, lactulose, allopurinol and pantoprazole; sodium 130 mEq/L, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, BP 106/64
warnings: Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV contrast where avoidable) during SBP
Avoid sedative drugs (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines) in hepatic encephalopathy

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the altered mental status to HE alone without a diagnostic paracentesis: SBP must be excluded in every patient with cirrhosis, ascites and encephalopathy.
Do not be reassured by a normal WBC and the absence of fever: the systemic inflammatory response is often blunted in cirrhosis, and SBP can present without fever or leucocytosis.

Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.

Do not perform a lumbar puncture: there is no sign of meningitis (no neck stiffness, photophobia or fever), a peritoneal source is identified, and the coagulopathy (INR 2.0, platelets 94) adds bleeding risk.
required_recommendations: Treat SBP with IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily (or cefotaxime), adjusted to culture, plus albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3; repeat paracentesis at 48 hours if there is no clinical improvement (EASL 2018).
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose (chronic heavy alcohol use).

Hold spironolactone and furosemide during SBP and monitor creatinine, sodium and urine output daily; reduce or stop propranolol if systolic BP falls below 90 mmHg, sodium falls below 130 mEq/L or kidney injury develops (EASL 2018; Baveno VII).
After this episode, give long-term antibiotic prophylaxis against recurrent SBP (norfloxacin 400 mg daily or ciprofloxacin) (EASL 2018).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 25 (EASL 2018); assess alcohol use with collateral and offer alcohol-use disorder treatment.
Stop pantoprazole unless there is a specific indication: proton pump inhibitors are associated with SBP and HE in cirrhosis (EASL 2022).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis warranting echocardiography in this presentation.
Amyloid PET has no role in workup of acute metabolic encephalopathy; reversible HE precipitated by SBP is the diagnosis under evaluation.
Alzheimer genetic panel has no role in HE workup; acute metabolic encephalopathy in a cirrhotic is the clinical question.

Lumbar puncture is not indicated — there is no clinical suspicion for meningitis (no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no fever, no focal signs). Performing LP without this indication, particularly in a coagulopathic patient (INR 2.0, platelets 94), risks procedural hemorrhage without diagnostic benefit.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 25), precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (ascitic PMN 412 cells/mm3)

differential.diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy without identified infection (hyponatremia, poor intake)
differential.key_features: Excluded as the whole explanation: ascitic PMN 412 cells/mm3 with Gram-negative rods identifies SBP as the precipitant.
Abstinence reported by family but unverifiable; serum ethanol undetectable; no tremor, autonomic instability or hyperreflexia.
INR 2.0 and platelets 94 raise the risk, but there is no focal deficit and non-contrast CT shows no blood.
Na 130 mEq/L is mild; it can contribute to confusion but does not explain grade II HE with asterixis.
Chronic alcohol use and two days without food; no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus; thiamine is given empirically.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh C (13: bilirubin 4.2 3, albumin 2.3 3, INR 2.0 2, moderate ascites 3, HE grade 2 2); MELD-Na 25 (creatinine 1.1, bilirubin 4.2, INR 2.0, sodium 130)

SBP commonly presents without fever and without peripheral leukocytosis in cirrhotic patients — up to 30% of episodes are afebrile and WBC may be normal or low (hypersplenism); the blunted inflammatory response is well-recognized but clinically dangerous if used to incorrectly exclude infection.

The diagnostic criterion for SBP is ascitic fluid PMN >= 250 cells/mm3, independent of culture result, fever, or peripheral WBC — culture-negative SBP (approximately one-third of episodes) is treated identically to culture-positive SBP once the PMN threshold is met.

Every cirrhotic with ascites presenting with altered mental status requires diagnostic paracentesis as part of the standard workup — infection is a major and potentially reversible precipitant of HE, and missing it is a significant safety event.

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

Albumin infusion alongside antibiotic therapy for SBP reduces the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome (type 1 AKI) and improves 90-day survival in patients meeting criteria; this is a time-sensitive intervention.
Propranolol may mask the tachycardic response to infection (blunting fever and HR rise), further contributing to the clinically subtle presentation of SBP in this patient.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal WBC and absence of fever do not exclude SBP in cirrhosis — the inflammatory response is frequently blunted by hypersplenism, immunosuppression from liver failure, and beta-blockade. Paracentesis is mandatory regardless of peripheral leukocyte count or temperature.
red_herrings.data_point: WBC 6.8 x10^9/L (within normal limits) and temperature 37.1°C (afebrile)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Reassure the agent that infection is absent and attribute AMS to HE alone without performing paracentesis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: An elevated ammonia neither confirms HE nor identifies the precipitant; in a patient with cirrhosis, ascites and encephalopathy, the precipitant work-up, paracentesis first, is still mandatory.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Treat elevated ammonia as sufficient explanation for AMS and close the precipitant workup without proceeding to paracentesis.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. G. is a 59-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and known moderate ascites who was brought to the emergency department by his daughter for three days of worsening confusion and progressive lethargy. His daughter reported that he had been increasingly difficult to rouse from sleep, was disoriented and repeating himself, and had stopped eating over the prior 48 hours. He had no witnessed vomiting, no hematemesis, no dark stools, and no gross change in urine output. She denied any recent alcohol consumption but was not fully certain, as the patient lived with her and had prior episodes of covert drinking. He had been compliant with his lactulose per his daughter's report. On presentation he was lethargic, disoriented to time, and unable to give a reliable history. He denied headache, neck stiffness, or photophobia. His daughter denied any focal limb weakness, facial droop, or new falls. He had no prior episodes of overt hepatic encephalopathy. Notably, he was afebrile on arrival. His abdomen was moderately distended with ascites and he had mild diffuse tenderness on palpation but no peritoneal signs. No source of infection was initially apparent. Chest radiograph was clear.

neurological_exam.additional: Mild jaundice in sclerae. Moderate ascites — abdomen diffusely distended, dull to percussion in flanks, shifting dullness present. Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness to palpation (non-localizing). No rigidity. No rebound. No guarding. Palmar erythema. Spider angiomata on chest. No caput medusae. No fetor hepaticus at time of initial exam.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to assess reliably due to encephalopathy.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal, briskly reactive bilaterally. Extraocular movements intact. No nystagmus. Facial symmetry intact. Gag reflex present.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to stand and walk safely; requires two-person assist.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Disoriented to time (date, day and month); oriented to place and person. Lethargic but arousable. Slowed, tangential speech. Unable to complete serial 7s. Bilateral asterixis present on sustained arm extension (6-8 flaps/min). No recall of 3 objects at 5 minutes.
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all extremities. Strength 4+/5 throughout, limited by poor cooperation. Mildly increased tone bilaterally. No focal weakness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws symmetrically to noxious stimuli. Light touch testing limited by cooperation.
